newsitem.title: USA: Union expects few layoffs in US Shell/Texaco deal.
newsitem.headline: Union expects few layoffs in US Shell/Texaco deal.

text.p: Union officials interviewed Tuesday said they expected few refinery workers to be laid off as a result of the agreement by Shell Oil Co and Texaco Inc to combine major elements of their U.S. refining activities in the Midwest and West.

"I've heard that if there are cuts most will be in management jobs where Shell and Texaco have overlapping areas," said Mike Maloney, financial secretary of Local 5-241 of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union.

Maloney said he represents 315 unionized workers at Texaco's 100,000-barrel-per-day refinery in El Dorado, Kansas. It is one of four Texaco refineries that will be merged with four Shell refineries to form a joint downstream operation.

"Texaco management have indicated to us that they don't anticipate any drastic manpower reductions" among refinery workers, Maloney said, adding he believed overlapping office workers and marketing staff were more likely to get pink slips.

The refineries to be merged include three in California, two in Washington state, one in Kansas, one in Illinois and one in Texas. Five of them, as well as several lubricants plants that will be swept into the venture, have OCAW workers.

In a prepared release released Tuesday, the companies said "there may be some reduction in workforce during the transition, but the expectation is that net job creation will ultimately result from long-term growth opportunities generated by the new venture."
Alan Barnes, secretary treasurer of OCAW Local 4-367, said he has few fears about his 100 members who work at Shell's 9,500 bpd lubricants plant in Deer Park, Texas.
"With attrition over the years, our hourly people are already stretched pretty thin. There's not much fluff to get rid of," he said.

"There's probably redundancies between the support staff in the companies. I think that's what they'll look at to cut -- purchasing and marketing people. They're more at risk than hourly people running the plant."
